content: Bellis perennis, commonly known as the Common Daisy, Lawn Daisy, or occasionally the English Daisy, is a species of daisy native to western, central, and northern Europe. It is often regarded as the archetypal daisy species, although the name daisy is shared by many related plants. In North America, where it has been widely naturalized, it is considered an invasive weed. This herbaceous plant features short creeping rhizomes and small, rounded or spoon-shaped evergreen leaves that measure 2–5 cm in length. Its flower heads are 2–3 cm in diameter and consist of white ray florets, often tipped with red, surrounding yellow disc florets. These flowers are borne on leafless stems that range from 2–10 cm in height, though they can occasionally grow up to 15 cm. Bellis perennis is classified as a dicotyledonous plant. The name daisy is believed to originate from the phrase day's eye, referring to the flower's behavior of closing its head at night and reopening in the morning. This etymology is supported by Chaucer, who referred to the daisy as the eye of the day. Additionally, Daisy is a common name for girls. Bellis perennis is resilient to mowing, which often leads to its classification as a weed in lawns. However, many people appreciate the aesthetic appeal of its flowers. Several cultivars and hybrids have been developed, featuring larger flower heads up to 5–6 cm in diameter and ray florets in shades ranging from light pink to purple-red. This plant is also widely used in homeopathic medicine. Herbalists employ Bellis perennis to address a variety of conditions, including kidney problems, rheumatism, arthritis, bronchitis, and diarrhea. It is known to possess astringent properties as well.
